templates.name: Blank completion, phrase options (word + preposition, a/an + word)
Blank completion, contrast clue (including received view then finding)
Blank completion, cause or consequence clue
Most nearly mean, underlined phrase or phrase options

items.passage: Kathrin Dausmann and colleagues found that the fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar hibernates for up to seven months inside tree holes where temperatures can exceed 30°C, conserving energy through the island’s long dry season, when food is scarce. The finding suggests that hibernation, traditionally associated with freezing winters, is not necessarily ______ cold.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Contingent on” means dependent on. The lemur hibernates for months in tree holes that can be hotter than 30°C, so in this animal hibernation clearly does not require cold. The text therefore concludes that hibernation, though long linked to freezing winters, does not necessarily depend on cold.

A.why_wrong: Saying hibernation is not necessarily “incompatible with” cold would mean it can occur in the cold, which nobody doubted and which the lemur study does not address. The finding is about hibernation happening in heat, so it shows hibernation does not depend on cold.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that hibernation could harm, or be “detrimental to,” cold; the study concerns whether hibernation requires cold, not any effect it has on temperature.

D.why_wrong: “Conducive to” means tending to bring about. Hibernation does not produce cold, and the text never discusses whether it might; it reports that the lemur hibernates even when its surroundings are hot.

sources.what: Dausmann et al. 2004 (Nature): fat-tailed dwarf lemurs (Cheirogaleus medius) hibernate about seven months in tree holes despite temperatures over 30°C, the first tropical primate hibernator

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Key C. Band 6 by plan. Clue: the second sentence’s conclusion follows from hibernation in heat; the reader must see that hibernation in 30°C tree holes shows it does not depend on cold, then pick the dependence phrase. Distractors: one reversal of the conclusion (incompatible with), two unsupported phrases that sound scientific. Simplified: the study also found that body temperature tracked tree-hole temperature in poorly insulated holes.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. Corrected ranks incompatible with 23,791, detrimental to 28,955, contingent on 17,762, conducive to 24,104 (4 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.37), but the negation is stated plainly (not necessarily) and two distractors fall to one fact (hibernation cannot harm or produce cold), the band-6 pattern; two steps (hibernation in 30°C holes, so not dependent on cold).

items.passage: Sri Lankan architect Minnette de Silva’s Karunaratne House in Kandy, completed around 1950, joined modernist forms with local crafts in what came to be called regional modernism. Because Geoffrey Bawa, now far better known for that approach, came to architecture several years later, historians increasingly regard de Silva as ______ Bawa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A forerunner is someone who comes before another and prepares the way. De Silva was already combining modernist design with local crafts around 1950, and Bawa, who later became famous for the same approach, came to architecture several years after that. So historians see de Silva as coming before Bawa in this approach, that is, as a forerunner of him.

B.why_wrong: A disciple learns from and follows a teacher. Because de Silva was working in this style before Bawa had even come to architecture, she could not have learned it from him; the text suggests the reverse order.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that de Silva and Bawa competed with each other for commissions or recognition. The reason it offers, that Bawa came to architecture several years later, concerns who came first, not competition.

D.why_wrong: A benefactor gives someone money or other help. Nothing in the text suggests that de Silva supported Bawa in any way; it links them by a shared approach and points out only that she used it first.

sources.what: Minnette de Silva, instigator of regional modernism, Karunaratne House (completed 1950, some sources 1951); overshadowed by Geoffrey Bawa, her contemporary but a latecomer to architecture (Apollo)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (architecture). Key A. Band 6 by plan. Frame: a/an + noun + of (the other hard B6 uses word + preposition). Steps: date of her house, Bawa came to architecture later, so she came first; then match precedence to forerunner, while disciple reverses the order. Kept within the sources: no claim that Bawa was influenced by her. Reviewer: C a rival of and D a critic of replaced with a competitor of and a benefactor of (same recipes) so all four options sit in one band (corrected 13,000 to 32,000).

fixes: option set was the band-5 pattern (key forerunner 25,769 the rarest, rival 3,703 and critic 4,842 under 10,000): C a rival of replaced with a competitor of (31,911), D a critic of with a benefactor of (13,044); why_wrong C and D rewritten

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target after the option swap. B6 a/an + noun frame, two steps (her house predates Bawa's start, so she came first; then precedence = forerunner, with disciple the order reversal). Options now one band: forerunner 25,769, disciple 13,554, competitor 31,911, benefactor 13,044; key not the rarest.

items.passage: Ethnographers have characterized some cultures as comfortable with lengthy silences between speakers and others as prone to continual overlapping talk, but the findings of linguist Tanya Stivers and colleagues suggest that such accounts are ______. Analyzing conversations in ten languages, the team discovered that speakers of every language avoided both overlap and prolonged silence; the languages did differ, but each one’s average gap between turns fell within a quarter second of the cross-language average.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Exaggerated” means made to seem larger than it really is. The ethnographers described dramatic differences between cultures, while Stivers’s team found that every language avoided overlap and long silences and that the languages differed only slightly in timing. The accounts described a real difference as much bigger than it is, so they were exaggerated.

A.why_wrong: If the accounts had been “corroborated,” or confirmed, the study would have found large differences in timing. Instead it found that every language avoided overlap and long silences, which goes against the accounts.

B.why_wrong: “Unfounded” would mean the accounts had no basis at all. The text says the languages did differ in their average gaps, just not by much, so the accounts overstated a real difference rather than inventing one.

C.why_wrong: “Belated” means coming too late. The text says nothing about when the ethnographic accounts appeared; it compares what they claimed with what the study found.

sources.what: Stivers et al. 2009 (PNAS): ten languages all avoid overlap and minimize silence; mean gaps differ within 250 ms of the cross-language mean; tempo differences lead to a subjective perception of dramatic differences in ethnographic reports

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics). Key D. Band 6 by plan. Two steps: the languages share the same pattern, and the clause “the languages did differ” rules out unfounded, leaving a difference in degree (exaggerated). The near miss (unfounded) fails on degree alone. The paper itself says the small tempo differences produce a perception of dramatic differences in ethnographic reports.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. B1 with a degree near miss (unfounded) ruled out only by 'the languages did differ', two steps. Ranks corroborated 22,317, unfounded 26,336, belated 11,697, exaggerated 6,194 (3 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.16); the plain key fits band 6, where keys run common (section 2 point 2).

items.passage: Though early evaluations of Moving to Opportunity, a 1990s experiment that offered families in high-poverty public housing vouchers to relocate to lower-poverty neighborhoods, suggested that its economic benefits were ______, Raj Chetty and colleagues later found that children who had relocated before age 13 went on to earn substantially more as adults than counterparts whose families had received no voucher.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Marginal” means small or barely noticeable. The sentence sets the early evaluations against Chetty’s finding with “Though,” and Chetty found that children who moved young later earned substantially more. For the two to contrast, the early evaluations must have suggested that the program’s economic benefits were small, or marginal.

A.why_wrong: “Deferred” means put off until later, which describes what Chetty found: the gains appeared years later, when the children were adults. Since “Though” sets the early evaluations against that finding, they cannot have suggested the same thing.

C.why_wrong: “Fungible” means interchangeable with something else of the same value, as money is. Nothing in the text concerns whether the benefits could be exchanged, and the word sets up no contrast with Chetty’s finding about the size of later earnings.

D.why_wrong: “Redistributive” means shifting income or wealth from some people to others. The text says nothing about whether the program moved money between groups; the contrast it draws is about how large the benefits were.

band7_moves: concessive Though frame with the blank on the view being challenged (as in e8fb0744 and 177ed7dc)
direction left implicit: the reader infers the early view from the later finding
the finding side’s trait (deferred) offered as the reversal, as commonplace is in e8fb0744
all four options past corrected rank 10,000, two unseen in both corpora

sources.what: Chetty, Hendren, and Katz (NBER w21156, AER 2016): moving to a lower-poverty area before age 13 raises college attendance and earnings; earlier MTO studies found no significant effect on adults’ earnings

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key B. Steps: (1) Though sets the early view against the finding; (2) the finding is about the size of later earnings, so the early view must be that benefits were small; the finding side’s own trait (deferred) is the reversal. Section 6 checks (corrected ranks): deferred 11,759; marginal 15,954; fungible and redistributive unseen (1,000,000); 4 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000, mean log above 4.5; rarest distractor unseen. Band-5 guard clear (key not the rarest). Concessive frame: yes. Simplified: the earlier null results were for adults and teenagers; the 31 percent figure is left out.

band7.why: Section 6 checks pass: deferred 11,759, marginal 5,487 corrected (34,666 raw), fungible and redistributive unseen: 3 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.95, rarest distractor unseen, key not the rarest (band-5 guard clear). B3 received view then finding with the blank on the received view and a concessive Though frame (both band-7 signals); deferred is the finding side's own trait, a reversal that needs the contrast to reject. Comparable to e8fb0744 (negligible, same corrected rank).

items.passage:
The following text is from W. Somerset Maugham’s 1919 novel The Moon and Sixpence. The narrator is watching Blanche Stroeve, who has left her husband, Dirk.

Her face was a mask that told nothing. Her hands lay on her lap motionless, one in the other loosely clasped. I knew from what I had heard that she was a woman of violent passions; and that injurious blow that she had given Dirk, the man who had loved her so devotedly, <u>betrayed</u> a sudden temper and a horrid cruelty.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “betrayed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: “Evinced” means showed clearly, and as used here “betrayed” means showed or revealed without meaning to. Blanche’s face “told nothing,” but the narrator knows she has “violent passions,” and the blow she gave Dirk let those passions be seen. The blow, in other words, evinced her sudden temper and cruelty.

A.why_wrong: “Betray” can mean to deceive someone, but here the object is “a sudden temper and a horrid cruelty,” and a blow cannot deceive a temper. The sentence is about what the blow showed about Blanche.

B.recipe: topic word from the scene, near miss (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: A blow might seem to stir up anger, but this blow was Blanche’s own, given out of the “violent passions” the narrator already knew she had. The temper came first and the blow showed it; the blow did not incite it.

C.why_wrong: “Betray” can mean to abandon someone, and Blanche has indeed left Dirk, which makes this tempting. But in this sentence the thing “betrayed” is her temper and cruelty, which the blow made visible, not something she deserted.

band7_moves: common target in a secondary sense (betrayed as revealed), as reserve and manifest in the band-7 models
two distractors are real senses of the target, one fitting the scene loosely (Deserted: she has left Dirk)
one topic word from the scene (Incited) that fails on cause and effect
key is a mid-frequency word (Exhibited), not the plain everyday synonym (Showed)

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #222, W. Somerset Maugham, The Moon and Sixpence (1919), chapter on the chess game with Strickland and Blanche; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1919, public domain). Key D. Target betrayed in its secondary sense (revealed unintentionally), with a contrast clue: the mask-like face told nothing, the blow told much. Two distractors are real senses of betray (deceive, desert), one fits loosely through the scene (she has deserted Dirk); one topic word (incited) fails on the order of cause and effect. Option ranks (corrected): Deceived 3,195; Incited 21,291; Deserted 2,227; Exhibited 4,538; mean log about 3.7, in line with CB’s band-7 meaning items (6557f7fc 3.88, 7f935017 3.84), which are mid-frequency: the band-7 lever in M1 is polysemy and loose-fitting senses, not rarity. Earlier in the novel Blanche slaps Dirk’s face, which is the blow referred to. Reviewer: key Exhibited (corrected 2,471, a plain everyday synonym) replaced with Evinced (14,486), a mid-frequency key as the M1 band-7 recipe asks; set now Deceived 3,195, Incited 21,291, Deserted 1,624, Evinced 14,486 (mean log 3.80, level with the CB band-7 M1 models).

fixes: key Exhibited (corrected 2,471, the plain everyday synonym section 5 says not to key) replaced with Evinced (14,486); explanation rewritten

band7.why: M1 band-7 recipe after the key swap: a common target (betrayed) in its secondary sense (revealed), key a mid-frequency word that is not a plain synonym (Evinced 14,486), two real senses of the target with scene hooks (Deceived, Deserted: she has left Dirk) and one topic word (Incited, fails on cause order). Set mean log 3.80, level with the CB band-7 M1 models (6557f7fc 3.88, 7f935017 3.84), which do not pass check 1 either; transferred sense and two steps (the mask face against the blow) meet check 5.

items.passage: Electric organs offer a striking example of evolutionary ______: such organs originated independently in at least six lineages of fish, including the electric eels of South America and the elephantfish of Africa, two groups that are only distantly related. Moreover, Jason Gallant and colleagues determined that the lineages relied on largely identical genes and developmental pathways to build their organs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: In evolution, convergence is the independent development of similar features in separate lineages. The text says electric organs arose separately in at least six lineages of fish, and that the lineages relied on largely the same genes to build them. Separate lineages arriving at the same kind of structure is an example of convergence.

B.why_wrong: Mimicry is one species coming to resemble another, usually to fool predators or prey. The fish in the text did not evolve electric organs to imitate one another; each lineage developed the organ on its own.

C.why_wrong: Atavism is the reappearance of a trait from a distant ancestor. The text does not say the organs were an ancestral trait that resurfaced; it says they arose separately in each lineage.

D.recipe: near synonym failing on one feature (CONNOT)
D.why_wrong: Homology is similarity between structures that were inherited from a common ancestor. The shared genes make this tempting, but the text says the organs originated independently in each lineage, so their similarity does not come from a shared ancestor.

band7_moves: colon and a described finding; key is the abstract category the examples instantiate
near-synonym distractor (mimicry) that fails on a single feature (resemblance for deception, not independent origin)
three of four options past corrected rank 10,000, rarest distractor (atavism) past 50,000

sources.what: Gallant et al. 2014 (Science): electric organs evolved independently six times in fish, built from muscle using largely the same genetic toolkit (UT Austin release)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (evolutionary biology). Key A. Colon then a described finding; the key names the abstract category the examples instantiate, as counterfactual, disparate and elasticity do in the models. Near miss: mimicry (resemblance between species, fails on purpose and on independence). Reversal: divergence. Section 6 checks (corrected ranks): convergence 20,154; mimicry 10,929; atavism 58,921; divergence 9,298; 3 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000, mean log about 4.27, rarest distractor past 50,000. Band-5 guard clear (key not the rarest, no two distractors under 10,000). Reviewer: second sentence said every lineage built its organ from muscle cells, stronger than the source (some lineages); now the shared genes and pathways only. D divergence (the mirror of the key) replaced with homology, a near synonym that fails on one feature (common ancestry against independent origin). Ranks by the review script: convergence 7,434 corrected (51,067 raw), mimicry 32,848, atavism 58,921, homology unseen.

fixes: passage said every lineage built its organ by modifying muscle cells; the source says some lineages evolved electrocytes from muscle, so the sentence now states only the shared genes and developmental pathways the source reports
D divergence (the antonym mirroring the key) replaced with homology, a near synonym failing on one feature (shared ancestry against independent origin); explanation and why_wrong updated
passage lengthened to the models’ median (53 to 59 words) with a clause that eels and elephantfish are only distantly related

band7.why: B4 example-pinned, key the abstract category (as counterfactual, elasticity). After the swap: convergence 7,434 corrected (51,067 raw), mimicry 32,848, atavism 58,921, homology unseen: 3 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000, mean log 4.79, rarest distractor unseen. Homology is the one-feature near synonym (shared ancestry against independent origin) that the shared-genes sentence makes tempting; no antonym pair left to give the key away.

items.passage: Until 2012, the oldest plant ever regenerated from ancient material had sprouted from a 2,000-year-old date palm seed, so considerably older tissue seemed unlikely to remain ______. Then Svetlana Yashina’s team cultivated flowering Silene stenophylla plants from fruit tissue that Ice Age ground squirrels had stored in Siberian permafrost approximately 32,000 years earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Viable” means able to live and grow. The previous record for growing a plant from ancient material was a 2,000-year-old seed, so tissue many times older seemed unlikely to still be capable of growth. The next sentence shows that this expectation was wrong: Yashina’s team grew flowering plants from tissue about 32,000 years old.

A.why_wrong: “Inert” means lifeless or inactive. Old tissue would be expected to be inert, so saying it seemed “unlikely to remain inert” reverses the logic; the surprise in the text is that ancient tissue could still grow.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns whether the tissue was poisonous; the record and the result it describes are both about growing plants.

D.why_wrong: The squirrels stored the fruit, presumably as food, which makes “palatable,” or pleasant to eat, tempting. But the text sets up a question about whether ancient tissue could still grow, and the answer it gives is that it grew into flowering plants, not that it could be eaten.

sources.what: Yashina et al. 2012 (PNAS): whole fertile Silene stenophylla plants regenerated from about 31,800-year-old fruit tissue from fossil squirrel burrows in Siberian permafrost; previous record 2,000-year-old date palm seeds from Masada

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany). Key B. Negated frame: “seemed unlikely to remain ______,” with the expectation overturned in the next sentence. Distractors: one reversal (inert), one unsupported (toxic), one topic echo (palatable, from the squirrels’ stored food). Rounded: 31,800 years to about 32,000.

items.passage: In the mid-twentieth century, weaving was frequently dismissed as merely decorative craftwork. Anni Albers, however, considered it ______ painting as an art form: she produced what she called “pictorial weavings,” abstract compositions intended to be framed and displayed on a wall rather than used as fabric.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be “on a par with” something is to be equal to it in standing. Albers rejected the idea that weaving was only decorative craftwork and made weavings to be framed and displayed like paintings. This shows she considered weaving equal to painting as an art form.

A.why_wrong: “Subordinate to” means lower in rank than. That describes the dismissive view the text says Albers rejected, not her own view; her pictorial weavings treated weaving as art in its own right.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Albers saw weaving as an introduction or first step toward painting; the text says she made finished weavings to be displayed as art.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Albers thought weaving endangered painting or competed to replace it; the text says she wanted her weavings viewed the way paintings are, as art.

sources.what: Anni Albers made “pictorial weavings,” hand-woven works made as artworks to be hung on the wall, not fabrics for everyday use (Tate exhibition guide)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (textile art). Key D. Clue after the colon restates the key (framed and displayed like paintings, not used as fabric); the contrast with “dismissed as merely decorative craftwork” rules out subordinate to. Distractors: reversal (subordinate to, the dismissive view she rejected), two unsupported (a prelude to, a threat to); a near miss such as indistinguishable from was dropped because, with “as an art form,” it was close to defensible. Mixed frames (on a par with, a prelude to) as in official items with mixed options.

items.passage: Library of Congress librarian Daniel Murray set out to ______ the published work of Black American writers for the 1900 Paris Exposition. Hoping to locate a copy of every book and pamphlet by a Black author, he compiled a bibliography of more than a thousand titles, hundreds of which were subsequently exhibited in Paris.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “inventory” something is to make a complete list of it. The text says Murray tried to find a copy of every book and pamphlet by a Black author and compiled a bibliography, or list, of more than a thousand titles. That effort to record all of these works is an inventory of them.

A.why_wrong: To censor writing is to suppress or remove it. Murray did the opposite: he searched out these works, listed them, and helped put hundreds on public display.

B.why_wrong: Because the works were shown in Paris, “translate” may be tempting, but the text never says Murray put any of them into French; it says he listed and gathered them.

D.why_wrong: To dramatize a work is to adapt it for the stage or to make it seem more exciting. Nothing in the text suggests Murray did either; his task was finding and listing the works.

sources.what: Daniel Murray’s Preliminary List of Books and Pamphlets by Negro Authors (1900): his aim was to secure every book and pamphlet by a Black author for the Exhibit of American Negroes at the Paris Exposition; books from the list were shown there and the list later grew past two thousand titles (sources give 1,100 for the 1900 list)

items.notes: Subject: history. Key C. Restatement in the next sentence (locate a copy of every book, compiled a bibliography). Distractors: reversal (censor), topic echo (translate, from Paris), unsupported (dramatize).

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Because globe skimmer dragonflies (Pantala flavescens) cannot reproduce in the Maldives, islands with almost no freshwater habitat for their larvae, the swarms that appear there each autumn must have ______ open ocean to arrive. Keith Hobson and colleagues supported this conclusion by tracing chemical signatures in the insects’ wings to rainwater in northern India.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “traverse” something is to travel across it. Since the dragonflies cannot have hatched in the Maldives, which lack fresh water for their young, they must have come from somewhere else, and the islands are surrounded by ocean. Hobson’s team traced the insects to northern India, so the swarms must have crossed, or traversed, the open ocean.

B.why_wrong: To skirt something is to go around its edge. The Maldives are islands in the open ocean, so dragonflies coming from India could not reach them by going around the ocean; they had to cross it.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the dragonflies polluted the ocean; the text is about how they reached the islands.

D.why_wrong: To evade something is to avoid it. Dragonflies arriving from India on islands surrounded by ocean could not have avoided the open water; the text’s reasoning requires that they crossed it.

sources.what: Hobson, Anderson, Soto, and Wassenaar 2012 (PLoS ONE): wing hydrogen isotopes of Pantala flavescens migrating through the largely waterless Maldives point to natal origins in northern India

items.notes: Subject: natural science (entomology). Key A. Cause in a Because clause (cannot reproduce in the Maldives), consequence in the main clause (must have crossed the ocean). Near miss: skirted (movement along an edge rather than across).

items.passage: Corals and many other invertebrates house photosynthetic algae inside their own cells, but vertebrate cells were thought to be ______ to such partners, since vertebrate immune systems were assumed to reject them. In 2011, however, Ryan Kerney and colleagues found algae living inside the cells of spotted salamander embryos.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Inhospitable” means unwelcoming, not offering a place to live. The text contrasts invertebrates, whose cells house algae, with vertebrates, whose immune systems were assumed to reject such partners. So vertebrate cells were thought to be inhospitable to algae, until Kerney’s team found algae inside salamander cells.

A.why_wrong: “Receptive” means willing to receive. The text says vertebrate immune systems were assumed to reject algae, so vertebrate cells were thought to be the opposite of receptive; “but” also sets them against the invertebrates that do house algae.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the algae were thought to harm vertebrate cells. The text says the immune system was assumed to keep algae out, which is about the cells rejecting algae, not being endangered by them.

D.why_wrong: “Indispensable” means absolutely necessary. The text never suggests vertebrate cells were thought to be essential to algae; it says such partnerships were thought not to occur in vertebrates at all.

sources.what: Kerney et al. 2011 (PNAS): Oophila algae found inside the cells of spotted salamander embryos; vertebrate immune systems were assumed to bar such intracellular partnerships

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biology). Key C. Contrast (invertebrates house algae, but vertebrates were thought not to) plus received view then finding (however, Kerney found). Distractors: reversal (receptive), two unsupported adjectives that take “to.”

items.passage: Researchers Ovul Sezer, Francesca Gino, and Michael Norton found that humblebragging, or disguising a boast as a complaint (“I’m so tired of being asked to give speeches”), tends to ______. In their studies, people who humblebragged were considered less likable than people who simply bragged.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “backfire” is to have the opposite of the intended effect. People humblebrag to seem modest and likable, but the researchers found that humblebraggers were considered less likable than people who bragged openly. The strategy produces the opposite of what its users want, so it tends to backfire.

A.why_wrong: The text says humblebraggers were considered less likable than people who simply bragged, so the strategy fails at what it is meant to do; it does not succeed.

C.why_wrong: To proliferate is to multiply or spread rapidly. The text says nothing about humblebragging becoming more common; it reports how people react to it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that humblebragging dies out or weakens over time; the finding is about its effect on how much people are liked.

sources.what: Sezer, Gino, and Norton 2018 (JPSP), “Humblebragging: A Distinct, and Ineffective, Self-Presentation Strategy”: humblebraggers are liked less than braggers and the strategy backfires because it seems insincere (HBS Working Knowledge)

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology). Key B. Restatement in the next sentence (judged less likable than plain braggers, the opposite of the aim). The sample complaint is an unattributed illustration, not a quotation from the paper.

items.passage: Filming a runner on a treadmill in slow motion, engineers Christopher Daily-Diamond, Christine Gregg, and Oliver O’Reilly found that the failure of a shoelace knot is remarkably ______. A knot can withstand dozens of strides, but once it begins loosening, it can unravel completely within seconds as the whipping free ends of the laces pull it apart.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Rapid” means happening very quickly. The engineers found that a knot can withstand dozens of strides but, once it begins loosening, can unravel completely within seconds. That quick collapse is what makes the failure rapid.

A.why_wrong: “Gradual” means happening slowly, step by step. The text stresses the opposite: once a knot begins loosening, it unravels completely within seconds.

B.why_wrong: The text does not discuss whether an untied shoelace causes harm; it describes how quickly the knot fails.

C.why_wrong: A knot cannot act on purpose, and nothing in the text suggests anyone unties it intentionally; the failure comes from the runner’s strides.

sources.what: Daily-Diamond, Gregg, and O’Reilly 2017 (Proc. R. Soc. A), “The roles of impact and inertia in the failure of a shoelace knot”: slow-motion video of a runner on a treadmill showed knot failure happens within seconds after gradual loosening (Berkeley News)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (engineering, mechanics). Key D. Restatement in the next sentence (unravel completely within seconds). Distractors: reversal (gradual), two unsupported adjectives.

items.passage: In 1952, Roy DeCarava became the first African American photographer awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship. The fellowship allowed him to ______ an entire year to his own work, and he spent that year photographing everyday life in Harlem, the New York City neighborhood where he was born.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “devote” time to something is to give that time entirely to it. The fellowship let DeCarava spend an entire year on his own photography, and he used the year to photograph daily life in Harlem. So the fellowship allowed him to devote an entire year to his work.

B.why_wrong: The text says DeCarava spent the year photographing Harlem, so he used the year for his own work rather than refusing it.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests DeCarava compared a year with his work; the text says he spent the year doing that work.

D.why_wrong: It makes no sense to say DeCarava borrowed a year to his work, and the text describes the fellowship as an award he won, not something he had to repay.

sources.what: Whitney Museum: in 1952 DeCarava became the first African American photographer to receive a Guggenheim fellowship; he recorded everyday life in his own neighborhood, Harlem

items.notes: Subject: humanities (photography). Key A. Restatement in the clause after the blank (spent that year photographing). Easy key in the official easy range.

fixes: source URL (NGA) returns 403; replaced with the Whitney Museum page, which states the Guggenheim first and the Harlem work

items.passage:
The following text is from Theodore Dreiser’s 1900 novel Sister Carrie. Hurstwood, who has lost his business, is searching the newspaper advertisements for employment.

He scanned the long column, which mostly concerned bakers, bushelmen, cooks, compositors, drivers, and the like, finding two things only which <u>arrested</u> his eye. One was a cashier wanted in a wholesale furniture house, and the other a salesman for a whiskey house. He had never thought of the latter.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “arrested” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “arrested” most nearly means caught. Hurstwood is scanning a long list of job advertisements, and only two of them attract his attention: a cashier’s job and a salesman’s job. To say they “arrested his eye” is to say they caught his eye.

B.why_wrong: “Arrested” can mean detained by the police, but here nothing is held in custody; the text is about two advertisements that drew Hurstwood’s attention.

C.why_wrong: A person who is arrested may be charged with a crime, but advertisements cannot charge someone’s eye. The text describes which job listings Hurstwood noticed.

D.why_wrong: Reading a long column might tire the eyes, but the text says only two listings stood out to Hurstwood, not that they strained his eyesight.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #233, Theodore Dreiser, Sister Carrie (1900), chapter 35; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1900, public domain). Key A. Target arrested in its attention sense, decided by its object (his eye) and by the next sentence naming the two listings. Distractors: two other senses of arrest (detain, charge), one unsupported word from the scene (strained eyes from scanning). Stopped and Halted are not offered.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Max Beerbohm’s 1911 novel Zuleika Dobson. Zuleika, whose beauty has drawn an enormous crowd, has climbed onto the roof of a barge moored on the river.

It looked very cool and gay, this roof, under its awning of red and white stripes. Zuleika moved to the side which <u>commanded</u> a view of the bank. She leaned her arms on the balustrade, and gazed down. The crowd stretched as far as she could see—a vista of faces upturned to her.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “commanded” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “commanded” most nearly means offered. Zuleika goes to the side of the roof from which she can look down at the bank, and from there she sees the crowd stretching as far as she can see. The side of the roof offered, or provided, a view of the bank.

A.why_wrong: “Commanded” often means ordered, but a side of a roof cannot give orders; the text is about what Zuleika could see from that side.

B.why_wrong: A person can command, or earn, respect, but a side of a roof does not earn a view. The text simply says that side looked out over the bank.

D.why_wrong: Something can command, or demand, attention or a high price, but a side of a roof does not demand a view; the sentence describes the view available from that side.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #1845, Max Beerbohm, Zuleika Dobson (1911), chapter on the boat races; excerpt adapted by removing one sentence ("Nests of red and white flowers depended along either side of it.")

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1911, public domain). Key C. Target commanded in its view sense, fixed by its object (a view of the bank) and by the next sentences (she gazed down at the crowd). All three distractors are other senses of command, the most common recipe for meaning items. Original double hyphen rendered as a closed em dash.

fixes: intro said riverboat; in the novel it is a college barge moored by the bank, so now a barge moored on the river

items.passage:
The following text is from G. K. Chesterton’s 1904 novel The Napoleon of Notting Hill. Adam Wayne, the novel’s idealistic protagonist, has been visiting the shops of his London neighborhood.

The man who <u>kept</u> the shop of curiosities had, indeed, enchanted him with a phrase. He was standing drearily at the door of his shop, a wrinkled man with a grey pointed beard, evidently a gentleman who had come down in the world.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “kept” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “kept” most nearly means managed. The man is described as standing at the door of “his shop,” so he is the one who runs the shop of curiosities. To keep a shop, in this sense, is to manage it.

A.why_wrong: To keep something from someone can mean to withhold it, but nothing is being held back from anyone here; the man is standing at the door of the shop he runs.

B.why_wrong: To keep something can mean to save it for later, but the text presents the man as the shopkeeper who runs the shop, not someone storing it away.

C.why_wrong: To keep someone can mean to delay them, as in keeping a person waiting, but here the object is a shop, and the man is the one who runs it.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #20058, G. K. Chesterton, The Napoleon of Notting Hill (1904), Book II, chapter 2; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1904, public domain). Key D. Target kept in its older sense (run a shop), fixed by its object and by “his shop” in the next sentence. All three distractors are other senses of keep. British spelling grey kept as in the source.

items.passage: Cuban filmmaker Sara Gómez’s feature film One Way or Another (1977) is ______ documentary and fiction: its invented love story, acted partly by professional performers, unfolds among real residents of Miraflores, a working-class neighborhood of Havana, who appear on screen as themselves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “A blend of” means a mixture of. The text explains that the film tells an invented love story, partly acted by professional performers, while also showing real residents of a Havana neighborhood as themselves. Combining fiction with documentary material in this way makes the film a blend of the two.

A.why_wrong: The film uses both a fictional story and real people appearing as themselves, so it embraces documentary and fiction rather than rejecting them.

B.why_wrong: A sequel continues an earlier work. The text does not mention any earlier film or story that One Way or Another continues.

D.why_wrong: A review evaluates other works. The text describes how the film combines two kinds of filmmaking, not a discussion of other films.

sources.what: Sara Gómez’s De cierta manera (One Way or Another), completed 1977, mixes documentary and fiction with professional and nonprofessional actors in Miraflores, a Havana housing development

items.notes: Subject: humanities (film). Key C. Restatement after the colon (invented love story among real residents playing themselves). Simplified: Gómez died in 1974 during production and the film was finished by others; not needed for the item.

fixes: Miraflores called a housing project on the edge of Havana; the source says a lower-class neighborhood of Havana, so now a working-class neighborhood of Havana

items.passage: Australian architect Glenn Murcutt designs houses that are highly ______ the local climate. Rather than relying on air-conditioning, his buildings have adjustable louvers, blinds, and wide eaves that residents can open, close, or angle throughout the day to let in cooling breezes and block the hot sun.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Responsive to” means reacting to. Murcutt’s houses have louvers, blinds, and eaves that residents can adjust to let in breezes and keep out the sun. Because the houses can be changed to suit the weather, they are responsive to the local climate.

A.why_wrong: Murcutt’s houses let breezes in and are adjusted to the sun, so they engage with the climate rather than being hidden from it.

C.why_wrong: A house cannot literally be aware of anything, and the text describes buildings designed around the weather, the opposite of ignoring it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Murcutt’s houses harm the climate; the text says they avoid air-conditioning by using breezes and shade.

sources.what: Lynn Becker on Glenn Murcutt: adjustable louvers inside, slatted blinds outside, natural airflow; of more than 500 houses only two are air-conditioned

items.notes: Subject: humanities (architecture). Key B. Restatement in the next sentence (adjustable louvers and blinds to let in breezes and block sun). Two reversals (hidden from, unaware of), one unsupported (damaging to); easy items often carry two reversals.

fixes: source URL (Britannica) returns 403; replaced with a page that states the louvers, blinds and lack of air-conditioning

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Emily Fairfax and Andrew Whittle found that during wildfires in the western United States, streams dammed by beavers tend to remain green while the surrounding landscape burns, because the water held behind the dams keeps the vegetation moist. These green corridors may therefore help ______ animals from the flames.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “shelter” means to protect or give safe cover. The text explains that beaver-dammed streams stay green and moist during wildfires while the land around them burns. Places that do not burn could give animals somewhere safe to go, so these corridors may help shelter animals from the flames.

A.why_wrong: The text describes green areas that stay unburned, not anything that carries animals away; nothing suggests the corridors remove animals from the fire.

B.why_wrong: It makes no sense to say the corridors distract animals from the flames; the text’s point is that the corridors stay green and do not burn.

C.why_wrong: The researchers measured how green the areas stayed, but the corridors themselves do not measure animals; the sentence is about what the unburned areas can do for wildlife.

sources.what: NASA Landsat: Fairfax and Whittle found beaver-dammed riparian zones keep green, living vegetation during wildfires because pond water keeps plants and soil lush; the patches can act as a refuge for flora and fauna

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Key D. Consequence clue: therefore, after the cause (corridors stay green and moist while the land burns). Three unsupported distractors, the easy-tier pattern; measure is a mild topic echo of the satellite study. The animal-refuge idea is stated as a possibility (may), as in the source.

fixes: source (UMN record) did not state the animal-refuge premise the key hinges on; replaced with the NASA Landsat article, which does
passage said the dams spread water across the valley floor; both sources say the dams store water, so now the water held behind the dams

items.passage: French designer Charlotte Perriand’s two years in Japan, beginning in 1940, ______ the furniture she created there. For example, after noticing a pair of sugar tongs fashioned from bamboo, she reinterpreted her celebrated steel chaise longue, a reclining chair, in bamboo.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “shape” something is to influence its form. The example shows Perriand noticing bamboo sugar tongs in Japan and then reinterpreting her steel chaise longue in bamboo. Her time in Japan therefore shaped the furniture she created there.

B.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that Perriand’s time in Japan held up her work; the example shows her making new furniture there.

C.why_wrong: The text does not say her stay replaced the furniture she made; it shows how what she saw in Japan influenced that furniture.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Perriand’s stay hid her furniture from view; the text describes how a bamboo object she noticed led her to remake a chair.

sources.what: Charlotte Perriand arrived in Japan in 1940 and left in 1942; bamboo sugar tongs she saw in Tokyo led her to remake her steel chaise longue in bamboo (Pen magazine)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (design). Key A. Example-pinned: For example introduces the instance that shows influence. Three unsupported distractors (easy pattern).

items.passage: Indian filmmaker Ritwik Ghatak repeatedly ______ the 1947 partition of Bengal in his work. His films Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960), Komal Gandhar (1961), and Subarnarekha, for example, all portray the lasting upheaval caused when the region was divided between India and what became East Pakistan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “revisit” a subject is to return to it again. The text lists three of Ghatak’s films, all made years after 1947, that each portray the upheaval the partition caused. Since he came back to the partition in film after film, he repeatedly revisited it.

A.why_wrong: The films listed came out in 1960 and 1961 and later, long after the 1947 partition, so they could not have predicted it.

B.why_wrong: The films portray the “lasting upheaval” the partition caused, which suggests it is treated as a painful event; nothing in the text suggests Ghatak praised it.

D.why_wrong: The text gives several films that all deal with the partition, so Ghatak did not avoid the subject; he returned to it again and again.

sources.what: Ritwik Ghatak’s Partition trilogy, Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960), Komal Gandhar (1961), and Subarnarekha, about the aftermath of the 1947 partition of Bengal and the people it displaced (Scroll.in)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (film). Key C. Example-pinned: three films instantiate repeated treatment. Subarnarekha left undated (sources give 1962 and 1965).

fixes: B celebrated replaced with praised: celebrated can also mean commemorated in art, a second sense close to the key, and the swap brings the batch key-longest rate to the official range

items.passage: Tallying the 1880 US census by hand took years, and officials feared that the 1890 count might not be completed before the next census began. Herman Hollerith’s tabulating machine, which detected holes punched in cards, made tallying far less ______: an operator could process approximately 7,000 cards daily, at least ten times faster than by hand.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Laborious” means requiring a great deal of time and effort. Counting by hand took years, while Hollerith’s machine let an operator process approximately 7,000 cards a day, at least ten times faster. The machine therefore made tallying far less laborious.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about mistakes in the count; its point is how much faster the machine was, so there is no reason to think it made tallying less accurate.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the machine made tallying more chaotic; an operator feeding cards through a machine thousands of times a day describes a quicker, not a less orderly, process.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests the machine made the results of tallying harder to foresee; the text compares how long the work took by hand and by machine.

sources.what: Computer History Museum: estimates warned the 1890 census would not be finished before the 1900 census began; an average operator processed about 7,000 cards a day, at least ten times faster than manual methods

items.notes: Subject: history (technology). Key B. Negated frame (far less ______) with the clue after the colon (ten times faster). Kept to the source: the 1880 count took years (sources say seven to eight); no six-week figure.

items.passage:
The following text is from Lafcadio Hearn’s 1904 short story “Yuki-Onna.” Minokichi, a young woodcutter, and Mosaku, an old woodcutter, have taken shelter from a snowstorm in a ferryman’s hut, where a mysterious woman dressed in white has just appeared and vanished.

He called to Mosaku, and was frightened because the old man did not answer. He <u>put out</u> his hand in the dark, and touched Mosaku’s face, and found that it was ice!
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “put out” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “put out” most nearly means extended. In the dark, Minokichi cannot see Mosaku, so he reaches toward him and touches his face. To put out a hand in this sense is to extend it, or stretch it out.

A.why_wrong: “Put out” can mean to douse, or extinguish, a fire or a lamp, and the mention of the dark makes this tempting. But Minokichi puts out his hand and then touches Mosaku’s face, so he is reaching, not putting out a light.

C.why_wrong: To put someone out can mean to inconvenience them, but here the object is Minokichi’s own hand, which he uses to touch Mosaku’s face.

D.why_wrong: To put out a book is to publish it, a sense that has nothing to do with a man reaching for his companion in a dark hut.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #1210, Lafcadio Hearn, Kwaidan: Stories and Studies of Strange Things (1904), “Yuki-Onna”; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story, 1904, public domain). Key B. Phrasal target put out in its physical sense, fixed by the object (his hand) and the next action (touched Mosaku’s face). All three distractors are other senses of put out; Doused is the most tempting because of “in the dark.” Single-word options, as the phrase target allows (M2 covers an underlined phrase or phrase options).
